title: How to Secure Your Online Banking: 9 Steps Banks Don't Tell You
excerpt: Bank fraud losses hit record highs every year. These nine steps will significantly reduce your risk of having your accounts drained — going beyond the basics your bank tells you.
content:
The Real Threat to Your Bank Account

Most online banking fraud doesn't involve sophisticated hacking. It involves stolen credentials, SIM swapping, social engineering calls, and malware on your device. Banks have excellent fraud detection, but once an attacker has your credentials and can receive your 2FA SMS, they can often move money before you know anything is wrong.

The good news: most of these attack vectors are preventable with the right setup. Here's what to do.

Step 1: Use a Strong, Unique Password

Your banking password should be used nowhere else and should be genuinely random — not a memorable phrase, not a password you've used before. Use our password generator to generate a 20+ character password mixing uppercase, lowercase, numbers, and symbols. Store it in a password manager — don't rely on memory.

Many bank websites cap passwords at 12-16 characters and don't allow special characters. That's frustrating, but use the maximum they allow and make it fully random.

Step 2: Use an Authenticator App, Not SMS

Most banks offer SMS-based 2FA. It's better than nothing, but SIM swapping — where an attacker convinces your mobile carrier to transfer your number — can bypass it. If your bank offers an authenticator app option, use it. If they offer a hardware key, even better.

If SMS is your only option, be extra cautious about social engineering: a call claiming to be from your bank asking you to read back a code they just texted you is a classic attack. The code proves you are trying to log in — don't give it to anyone.

Step 3: Set Up Account Alerts

Enable every alert your bank offers: transactions over a threshold you set (even $1 to catch small test charges), login alerts, password change alerts, and new payee additions. These alerts should go to your email and your phone. They won't prevent fraud, but they let you react in minutes rather than days.

Step 4: Use a Dedicated Email Address

Create an email address used only for banking — not shared anywhere public, not used for newsletters or shopping. If attackers scrape your email from a data breach, they won't know this address exists. This dramatically reduces the attack surface.

Step 5: Never Bank on Public Wi-Fi

Public Wi-Fi in coffee shops, airports, and hotels is an easy interception point. If you must check your account when traveling, use your phone's cellular data or a VPN. A VPN encrypts your traffic even on compromised networks. NordVPN (linked on our recommended tools page) is a reliable option.

Step 6: Check Your Linked Accounts and Payees Regularly

Log into your bank account monthly and review: linked external accounts, saved payees, and any pending payment authorizations. Attackers who get into a bank account sometimes add a new payee and wait days before initiating a transfer, hoping you won't notice. Catching a new unauthorized payee is much easier than recovering transferred funds.

Step 7: Freeze Your Credit

A credit freeze at all three bureaus (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion) prevents anyone from opening new credit accounts in your name — even if they have your Social Security number. It's free, reversible, and doesn't affect your existing accounts. This is particularly important if your personal information has appeared in any data breach. Freeze your credit at each bureau's website directly.

Step 8: Keep Your Devices Clean

Keyloggers and banking trojans steal credentials before they even reach your bank's server — they capture what you type. Keep your operating system and browser updated (updates patch security vulnerabilities), use an antivirus on Windows, and be very careful what you install. On your phone, only install banking apps from official app stores.

Step 9: Know Your Bank's Actual Phone Number

Save your bank's official customer service number in your phone — get it from the back of your debit card or the bank's official website. If you ever receive a call claiming to be from your bank, hang up and call that saved number directly. 'Vishing' (voice phishing) attacks often create urgency ('your account is being drained right now') to get you to stay on the line and comply.

Recommended Tools

A password manager is the foundation of financial security. NordPass generates strong passwords and includes a breach scanner that checks if your email has appeared in leaked databases. 1Password offers Watchtower, which flags weak and compromised passwords across all your accounts. Both are reviewed in detail on our recommended tools page.
